title: Too Precise to Be True
objective: After this level you can explain how a number can look more exact than the measurement behind it, using the 98.6 degree fever line.
summary: The 98.6°F fever-chart line comes from Wunderlich's round 37°C, converted to Fahrenheit. The decimal came from the formula, not a sharper thermometer; a 1992 study found an average of 98.2°F.

cards.headline: 98.6°F looks measured to a tenth of a degree. It never was.
cards.body: That famous line on fever charts goes back to a German doctor's book from 1868. His number was a round 37°C. The .6 turned up when someone converted it.

cards.headline: A huge study, a round number
cards.body: Carl Wunderlich reportedly analyzed over a million underarm readings from some 25,000 patients. The average he gave for healthy adults was 37°C. Written as 37, that's a number to the nearest whole degree: it could stand for anything from 36.5°C to 37.5°C. The digits you write down are a promise about how sharp the measuring was.

cards.headline: Where the .6 came from
cards.body: To turn Celsius into Fahrenheit, multiply by 1.8 and add 32. Do that to 37 and you get exactly 98.6. The decimal comes from the formula, not from a better thermometer, and a calculation can't make a number more precise than its measurement. That 36.5 to 37.5 range is 97.7°F to 99.5°F. Tellingly, NIST's table of everyday temperatures lists body temperature as 37°C and 99°F.

cards.fact: When researchers measured again in 1992, the average was 98.2°F.
cards.context: A University of Maryland team took 700 oral readings from 148 healthy adults. The average was 36.8°C (98.2°F), and exactly 98.6°F came up in only 56 of the 700 readings. A number's decimals only mean something if the measurement behind them was that sharp.

questions.prompt: Wunderlich's 1868 average body temperature was the round Celsius number _____.
questions.explanation: Wunderlich gave 37°C, which converts to exactly 98.6°F.

questions.prompt: Why does "98.6°F" look more precise than the measurement behind it?

options.label: Fahrenheit thermometers are always more accurate
options.rationale: The scale doesn't add accuracy; the decimal came from a formula.

options.label: Its decimal came from converting a round 37°C
Wunderlich measured to a hundredth of a degree
The 1992 study added the decimal
options.rationale: The 98.6 came from converting 37°C long before 1992.

questions.explanation: 37 × 1.8 + 32 = 98.6. The .6 is arithmetic, and a calculation is never more precise than the measurement it starts from.

questions.prompt: The 1992 study found 98.6°F in 56 of 700 readings. Using Level 2's method, what percent is that?

options.rationale: That's the count, not the share.

questions.explanation: 56 ÷ 700 = 0.08; move the decimal point two places and you get 8%.
